entities.name: Clerkship peer workplace learning
observations: Question concerns whether medical students learn through peer groups during clinical clerkships.

entities.name: Clerkship peer learning exists
observations: In a qualitative survey of 54 clerkship students, formal and informal peer groups supported clinical expectations, patient and supervisor interactions, rotation transitions, implicit rules, and benchmarking of knowledge and skills.
Evidence is self-reported and qualitative, with no objective learning outcomes.

entities.name: Peer learning in clinical work
observations: A focused ethnography across five clinical departments observed peer-assisted learning used during authentic clinical activity to advance clinical reasoning.
Peer learning was often implicit; inconsistent facilitation and competitive or individualistic cultures could inhibit participation.

entities.name: Paired consultation pilot
observations: A two-month paired-consultation pilot with 41 students was judged successful and linked peer observation with clinical-reasoning learning.
Proposed mechanisms included psychological safety, reciprocal vulnerability, shared responsibility, autonomy, flexibility, supervisor support, and learner community.

entities.name: Peer workplace knowledge transfer
observations: Peer-to-peer handoffs across three clerkship rotations transmitted norms, expectations, tasks, logistics, learning opportunities, and strategies.
Patient-care discussion was rare and outcomes beyond perceived transition support were not measured.

entities.name: Clerkship co-regulation networks
observations: A social-network study of 403 clinical-training students found peers involved in learning goals, strategies, reflection, and self-evaluation.
Peer use declined across training years as supervisor engagement increased, suggesting a changing rather than absent peer role.

entities.name: Longitudinal peer continuity
observations: A review of 53 longitudinal community and hospital placement studies identified continuity of peer groups as a recurring mechanism associated with successful longitudinal placements.
The review did not isolate peer-learning effects and relied substantially on opinions or assessment results.
